passages.happening:
‘Jonah, however, was greatly displeased, and he became angry’ (verse 1). He prays to the LORD, and at last he says why he ran. Was this not what he said in his own country? That is why he fled toward Tarshish. ‘I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion’ (verse 2), one who relents from sending disaster.

‘And now, O LORD, please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live’ (verse 3). The LORD replies, “Have you any right to be angry?” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Jonah's anger makes sense against the history he knew. Assyria was the most feared military power of the day, and its kings boasted in their inscriptions of the cruelty they inflicted on rebels and conquered peoples. Within a few decades of Jeroboam II's reign, Assyria would destroy Jonah's own nation and take Samaria in 722 BC. A prophet who suspected that a spared Nineveh would one day devour his people had real reasons for his dread.

His prayer quotes Israel's central confession about God's character, first spoken by the LORD to Moses at Sinai after the golden calf: gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion. The confession is echoed often in the Old Testament. Jonah recites it as a complaint. The God who forgave Israel after the calf has forgiven Nineveh, and Jonah cannot bear it.

Jonah's wish to die is recorded honestly, as the Bible records Elijah's under the broom tree. God does not scold him for it. He asks him a question.
passages.later: God proclaimed his name to Moses: ‘The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness’ (Exodus 34:6). Elijah also prayed under a broom tree that he might die (1 Kings 19:4).
passages.hard:
How should Jonah's prayer to die be read?

Jonah's words come out of anger and despair, and the book does not hide them. He says it twice (verses 3 and 8). The story does not approve them, and it does not shame him for them either. God answers with a question, and then with patience: shade, a lesson, another question. The book's concern is Jonah's heart, and the God who keeps speaking to him.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Jonah was angry that God was so merciful. Ask whether there is anyone you would be angry to see God forgive. And God answered Jonah's anger with a question. Ask what question God might be asking you.

passages.t: A plant, a worm, and a question
passages.happening:
Jonah leaves the city and sits down east of it. He makes himself a shelter and sits in its shade to see what will happen (verse 5). The LORD God appoints a vine to grow up over him and give him shade, ‘and Jonah was greatly pleased with the plant’ (verse 6). At dawn God appoints a worm, and the plant withers (verse 7). When the sun rises, God appoints a scorching east wind. The sun beats on Jonah's head until he grows faint and wishes to die (verse 8).

God asks whether Jonah has any right to be angry about the plant, and Jonah says he is angry enough to die (verse 9). The LORD says that Jonah cared about the plant, which he did not tend or grow, which sprang up in a night and died in a night (verse 10). ‘So should I not care about the great city of Nineveh, which has more than 120,000 people who cannot tell their right hand from their left, and many cattle as well?’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The shelter Jonah builds is a booth of branches, like those used at harvest and the Feast of Booths. Such booths gave poor protection from the sun, so the plant gives real relief. Its identity is uncertain. Many suggest the castor-oil plant, a fast-growing shrub with broad leaves; the ancient Greek translation had a gourd, and Jerome chose ivy. The scorching east wind is the hot, dry wind from the desert that can wither plants in a day.

The verb appointed ties this chapter to the fish of chapter 1: God appoints a plant, a worm and a wind. God's argument runs from the lesser to the greater. If Jonah pities a plant he did not make, should God not pity a city of people and animals he did make?

The figure of 120,000 is a round number for a great city. Whether it counts the whole population, or only young children, if those who cannot tell their right hand from their left are children, is debated. The book ends with a question. Among the prophets only Nahum also does, and Nahum's last question is also aimed at Assyria.
passages.later: A psalm says, ‘The LORD is good to all; His compassion rests on all He has made’ (Psalm 145:9). Nahum closes his book with a question to the king of Assyria (Nahum 3:19).
passages.hard:
Why does the book end with a question, and no answer from Jonah?

The ending is deliberate. The book does not say whether Jonah gave up his anger, because the question is aimed past Jonah at the reader. Many interpreters think the first readers, whether Israelites in the eighth century or Judeans after the exile, were being asked to face their own resentment of God's mercy toward their enemies. Some suggest that the book itself, which portrays Jonah so unflatteringly, shows that Jonah or those around him later accepted God's point. Others note that the question works best unanswered, leaving each reader to give their own reply.

On both readings the book closes with God's compassion. Jonah's resentment is a warning to every reader of every people, and it is never a reason to blame the Jewish people, whose own Scripture tells this story against its own prophet.
passages.asks: Jonah grieved for a plant and not for a city. Ask what you grieve over, and what you have stopped caring about. And the question at the end is put to you. How will you answer it?
